keyIdeas.text: 25 772 года, наклон 23,44°, момент Луны и Солнца на экваториальном вздутии $1{,}8\cdot10^{22}$ Н·м

where: Велосипедное колесо на верёвке: ось не падает, а обходит круг за 9,4 секунды
Пуля с нарезом и фрисби: нулевой момент сохраняет направление оси, и тело не кувыркается
Гирокомпас и авиационный гироскоп: ось помнит направление, а уход считается по той же $\Omega = M/(I\omega)$
Прецессия земной оси: 50,3 угловой секунды в год, смена полярной звезды, сдвиг зодиака на знак
Магнитно-резонансный томограф: спин протона прецессирует в поле 1,5 Тл с частотой 64 МГц
memo.watchOut: Три ловушки. Первая — думать, что $\vec L$ смотрит туда, куда бегут точки тела; он смотрит вдоль оси, и правило правой руки тут не украшение, а определение. Вторая — ждать, что быстро раскрученный волчок и вбок пойдёт быстрее; всё наоборот, $\omega$ в знаменателе. Третья — применять формулу к медленному волчку: она верна только при $I\omega^{2} \gg mga$, а ниже порога $\sqrt{mga/I}$ прецессия сравнивается с собственным вращением и никакого постоянного наклона уже нет.

quiz.q: Ось раскрученного волчка наклонена, вес тянет центр масс вниз, момент относительно острия не равен нулю. Почему же ось не опускается?
options: Момент горизонтален: он не может ни изменить длину $\vec L$, ни убавить его вертикальную составляющую, а опускание оси требует одного из двух
Момент веса уравновешен моментом реакции опоры, так что суммарный момент равен нулю
Возникающая при вращении центробежная сила поднимает ось и компенсирует вес
Ось на самом деле опускается, просто настолько медленно, что за время наблюдения это незаметно
quiz.why:
Наклон оси задан отношением вертикальной проекции $L_z$ к длине $L$. Момент горизонтален, значит его вертикальная проекция нулевая и $L_z$ не меняется; момент перпендикулярен $\vec L$, значит не меняется и длина. Отношение постоянно, наклон заперт, свободен только азимут.

Ответ про уравновешенные моменты проверяется в одну строку: реакция опоры приложена в самой точке опоры, её плечо относительно этой точки равно нулю, момента она не даёт вовсе. Вариант с центробежной силой не годится потому, что никакой такой силы в неподвижной системе отсчёта нет — сила инерции появляется только при переходе во вращающуюся систему, и об этом третий параграф; к тому же она была бы направлена от оси, а не вверх. Вариант «опускается незаметно» описывает реальный волчок, но по другой причине: настоящая ось действительно медленно садится, однако из-за трения, которого в нашем выводе нет, а идеальный волчок держит наклон строго вечно.
quiz.hint: Опускание оси — это рост угла $\theta$, то есть уменьшение $\cos\theta = L_z/L$. Посмотрите, какие две величины должны для этого измениться, и спросите, умеет ли горизонтальный момент менять хоть одну из них.

quiz.q: Тот же волчок раскрутили вдвое быстрее — всё остальное без изменений. Что произойдёт со скоростью прецессии?
options: Уменьшится вдвое
Вырастет вдвое
Не изменится: момент силы тяжести тот же
Вырастет вчетверо
quiz.why:
$\Omega = mga/(I\omega)$ — собственная угловая скорость стоит в знаменателе, поэтому прецессия обратно пропорциональна раскрутке. Понять это можно и без формулы: за время $dt$ момент даёт то же самое приращение $d\vec L = \vec M\,dt$, но поворачивает оно теперь вдвое более длинный вектор, а значит на вдвое меньший угол.

Вариант «вырастет вдвое» — самая частая интуитивная ошибка в теме: кажется, что быстрый волчок должен и вбок бежать быстрее. Вариант «не изменится» верен для момента, но не для прецессии: числитель действительно тот же, изменился знаменатель. Проверить всё это можно и на глаз — умирающий волчок мечется по столу гораздо быстрее свежераскрученного, хотя момент тяжести у него ровно тот же.
quiz.hint: Выпишите формулу и посмотрите, в числителе или в знаменателе стоит $\omega$. Потом проверьте себя наблюдением: как ведёт себя волчок перед самым падением, когда вращение почти село?

quiz.q: Своими словами: почему момент, перпендикулярный вектору $\vec L$, не может изменить длину этого вектора, а только поворачивает его?
quiz.why:
Приращение вектора можно разложить на две части: направленную вдоль самого вектора и направленную поперёк. Только первая удлиняет или укорачивает, вторая исключительно поворачивает. Если приращение целиком перпендикулярно, продольной части просто нет, и длина остаётся прежней.

Формально это одна строка: производная квадрата длины равна удвоенному скалярному произведению вектора на его производную, а скалярное произведение перпендикулярных векторов равно нулю. Верно и обратное утверждение — если длина постоянна, производная обязана быть перпендикулярна.

Полезно заметить, что вектор тут может быть любым. То же рассуждение объясняет, почему сила, перпендикулярная скорости, не меняет её модуль: отсюда равномерное движение по окружности и отсюда же то, что магнитная сила не совершает работы.
quiz.hint: Разложите приращение на две составляющие — вдоль вектора и поперёк — и спросите, за что отвечает каждая. Или посчитайте производную от $\vec L \cdot \vec L$.

quiz.q: Велосипедное колесо массой 2,0 кг с моментом инерции $I = 0{,}245$ кг·м² раскручено до $\omega = 30$ рад/с и подвешено за конец оси на расстоянии $a = 0{,}10$ м от центра колеса. Какова угловая скорость прецессии? Ответ в рад/с, $g = 9{,}81$ м/с².
quiz.why:
$\Omega = mga/(I\omega) = 2{,}0 \cdot 9{,}81 \cdot 0{,}10 / (0{,}245 \cdot 30) = 1{,}962/7{,}35 = 0{,}267$ рад/с. Период обхода оси $T = 2\pi/\Omega = 23{,}5$ с — почти полминуты на круг.

Проверка без калькулятора: в седьмом шаге при плече 0,25 м вышло 0,667 рад/с. Плечо здесь в 2,5 раза меньше, а входит оно в формулу линейно, значит и ответ должен быть в 2,5 раза меньше: $0{,}667/2{,}5 = 0{,}267$. Сошлось.

Заодно проверьте условие быстрого волчка: $\sqrt{mga/I} = \sqrt{1{,}962/0{,}245} = 2{,}8$ рад/с при рабочих 30 — запас более чем десятикратный, формула применима уверенно.
quiz.hint: Всё есть прямо в формуле $\Omega = mga/(I\omega)$: подставьте числа и не забудьте, что $a$ — это расстояние от точки подвеса до центра масс, а не радиус колеса.

en.title: Angular Momentum and the Gyroscope
en.subtitle: Section 2 · Why a spinning top doesn't fall, but turns sideways
intro: Spin a top and tilt it. From everything we know so far, it should fall: the weight is applied at the center of mass, the center of mass hangs away from the pivot point, there is a lever arm, there is a torque—and nothing opposes that torque. The support pushes exactly at the tip, its lever arm is zero, and it provides no torque. The top must fall. It doesn't.

Instead of falling, something stranger happens: the tilt of the axis holds, and the axis itself slowly circles the vertical. The answer 'the spinning holds it' explains nothing until we say what the spinning actually does. The explanation turns out to be entirely geometric, and no new force is needed. A rotating body has a vector—angular momentum—that points along its axis. Gravity adds to this vector an increment directed along its torque. And the torque of gravity is perpendicular to both the vector and the vertical at once. These two perpendicularities lock the tilt of the axis in place.

Next, we'll get $\vec L = I\vec\omega$, rewrite the rotation equation from the first section in vector form, derive the precession rate $\Omega = mga/(I\omega)$, and discover that the tilt of the axis doesn't appear in it at all—it canceled along the way. Then we'll test the formula on a bicycle wheel, where the axis circles in nine and a half seconds, and on Earth, where the same formula gives twenty-six thousand years.
en.standNote:
Switch the stand to 'Gyroscope' mode. The shape, mass, and radius are the same as in the first section—they still combine to give the moment of inertia $I$. Three sliders have been added: initial angular velocity $\omega_0$, lever arm $a$ from the pivot point to the center of mass, and tilt of the axis $\theta$. The stand calculates and displays four numbers: $L = I\omega$, torque $M = mga\sin\theta$, precession rate $\Omega$, and the period of the axis's circuit.

Make exactly two movements on it. First: drag the tilt slider from 10 to 80 degrees. The torque changes almost sixfold—the sine grows from 0.17 to 0.98—but $\Omega$ doesn't budge. This is the test of step 6, where the sine canceled, and it's the most unexpected result of the section: a steeply tilted top circles the vertical at exactly the same rate as a nearly vertical one. Second movement: drag $\omega_0$ from 5 to 50 rad/s. Precession doesn't speed up; it slows down—by exactly the same factor.

At the defaults (hoop, $m = 2.0$ kg, $R = 0.35$ m, $\omega = 30$ rad/s, $a = 0.25$ m) the stand shows $I = 0.245$ kg·m², $L = 7.35$ kg·m²/s, $\Omega = 0.667$ rad/s, and a period of 9.4 s. The torque depends on the tilt: with the axis horizontal it's the full $mga = 4.90$ N·m, at a 30-degree tilt it's half that, 2.45 N·m—but $\Omega$ is the same in both cases. The same numbers are calculated by hand in step 7.

formula.name: Angular momentum and precession rate
formula.alsoKnown: Moment equation in vector form; formula for regular precession of a heavy symmetric top. For the Earth, the same phenomenon is called the precession of the equinoxes

authors.what: compared his measurements of the position of Spica with the records of Timocharis made a century and a half earlier and found that the vernal equinox point creeps along the ecliptic by at least a degree per century. The caution in the wording was appropriate: the true rate is 1.4 degrees per century. He discovered the phenomenon but did not know the cause.

in the third book of the Principia explained the precession of the equinoxes by the attraction of the Moon and Sun on the equatorial bulge of the Earth. This is the first calculation of a gyroscope in history—and it was done on a planet, a century and a half before a gyroscope was assembled on a table.

in 'Theory of the Motion of Rigid Bodies' wrote the equations of rotation in body-fixed axes, introduced the principal axes of inertia and the angles bearing his name; from these equations precession and nutation emerge as particular solutions.
built a fast rotor in a gimbal mount, showed that its axis holds its direction while the room turns with the Earth, and gave the device its name: gyroscope, 'one who watches the rotation'.

formula.story:
Between the discovery and the explanation here lie eighteen centuries, and between the explanation and the correct explanation another sixty years. Newton in the Principia obtained an almost correct value for the precession of the Earth's axis, but made two errors along the way: he thought the Moon acts on the Earth's bulge about four and a half times stronger than the Sun, whereas the true ratio is a little over two, and at the same time he incorrectly estimated the bulge itself. The errors partially canceled each other, and the answer came out close to the truth. A rigorous derivation was given by Jean le Rond d'Alembert in 1749, and it is from him that the theory of precession is usually counted as a calculation rather than a guess.

The instrument appeared later than the theory. In 1851 Foucault demonstrated the Earth's rotation with a pendulum, and the next year he wanted to show the same thing without a long wire and a high dome. He took a heavy disk, spun it up to several hundred revolutions per second, and suspended it in a gimbal mount where no torque could reach it. The axis held its direction while the whole laboratory slowly turned relative to it. The experiment was inconclusive for a purely engineering reason: friction in the bearings ate the rotation within a few minutes, and nothing could be measured quantitatively. The name remained. Half a century later, Hermann Anschütz-Kaempfe took on a task for which a magnetic compass is completely unsuitable—navigation inside the steel hull of a submarine—and in 1908 built a working gyrocompass. From that moment, the gyroscope turned from a demonstration toy into an instrument without which no airplane flies and no rocket reaches orbit.

symbols.note: a vector; when rotating about a principal axis, it is directed along the axis by the right-hand rule, not in the direction the points of the body run.

symbols.what: moment of inertia about the axis of rotation
symbols.note: taken ready-made from the first section: $I = kmR^2$, where $k$ is 1 for a hoop, ½ for a disk, ⅖ for a sphere.
also a vector along the axis; for a symmetric body rotating about a principal axis, $\vec L$ and $\vec\omega$ are parallel—in general they are not.

symbols.what: torque of external forces about the pivot point
symbols.note: for a heavy top this is the torque of weight; the reaction of the support is applied at the pivot point itself, its lever arm is zero, so it produces no torque.
the rate at which the axis goes around the vertical; do not confuse with $\omega$—for a fast top, $\Omega$ is tens and hundreds of times smaller.

symbols.what: angle of inclination of the axis to the vertical
symbols.note: does not enter the final formula: it cancels out. A vertical top ($\theta = 0$) does not precess at all—there is no torque.

symbols.what: distance from the pivot point to the center of mass
symbols.note: measured along the axis; the farther the center of mass from the pivot, the greater the torque and the faster the precession.
enters only through the torque of weight; in weightlessness $M = 0$, there is no precession, the axis simply holds its direction.

derivation.title: Rigorous derivation
derivation.lead: From the first section, we need exactly two things: the definition of moment of inertia $I$ and the equation of rotation $M = I\varepsilon$. Both are taken as given; we will not rediscover them. Everything else in this derivation is not physics but vector geometry: two perpendicularities and one arc.

steps.text:
Consider a body rotating about a fixed axis with angular velocity $\omega$. Each of its points has momentum $m_i v_i$ and lever arm $r_i$ — the distance to the axis. The sum of the products of momentum and lever arm is called the angular momentum about the axis. Substituting $v_i = \omega r_i$ from the first section, the familiar sum factors out: it is the same moment of inertia $I$.

But $L$ is not a number; it is a vector, and its direction is the source of half the confusion in this topic. It points ALONG THE AXIS, not in the direction the body's points are moving. The choice is not arbitrary: the axis direction is the only direction in the body that rotation leaves in place; all others rotate with it, and only along the axis can you draw an arrow so that it does not run away. Which way along the axis is given by the right-hand rule: curl your fingers in the direction of rotation, and your thumb points along $\vec L$.
steps.latex: L = \sum_i m_i v_i r_i = \sum_i m_i \omega r_i^{2} = \Bigl(\sum_i m_i r_i^{2}\Bigr)\,\omega = I\omega, \qquad \vec L = I\vec\omega
steps.figCaption: Points on the rim run in circles, but the vector $\vec L$ points along the axis: it is the only direction that rotation leaves in place

steps.text:
Differentiate this equality with respect to time. The body is rigid, the axis is the same, so $I$ is constant and comes out of the derivative. What remains is the derivative of angular velocity — angular acceleration $\vec\varepsilon$ — and the product $I\vec\varepsilon$ we already know: it is the moment of external forces, the equation of rotation from the first section.

Formally, we have written nothing new. Substantively, we have written everything. The scalar form $M = I\varepsilon$ can answer exactly one question: faster or slower. The vector form also answers the question "which way will the axis turn," and that is precisely what concerns us. It must be read literally and without corrections from common sense: in time $dt$, the vector $\vec L$ receives an increment $d\vec L = \vec M\,dt$ directed WHERE THE MOMENT POINTS. Not where $\vec L$ itself points, and not where the force pulls.
steps.latex: \frac{d\vec L}{dt} = I\,\frac{d\vec\omega}{dt} = I\vec\varepsilon = \vec M \qquad \Longrightarrow \qquad d\vec L = \vec M\,dt
steps.figCaption: The increment adds to the vector by the parallelogram rule and is directed along the moment, not along $\vec L$ itself

steps.text:
First, consider the simple case: no external moment. Then $\vec L$ is constant, and constancy of a vector means constancy of two things at once: magnitude and direction. The magnitude is remembered more often (the figure skater pulling in her arms is analyzed in the topic "Conservation Laws"), but in engineering the second half almost always works: a freely flying spinning body holds its axis in space.

A rifled bullet: a twist rate of 25 centimeters at a speed of 800 m/s gives 3200 revolutions per second, i.e., $\omega \approx 2\cdot10^{4}$ rad/s — one hundred ninety thousand revolutions per minute. The axis of such a bullet holds along the trajectory, and the bullet does not tumble but goes nose-first. A frisbee at ten revolutions per second holds its plane and therefore glides rather than falls. A satellite spun about an axis aimed at a desired point maintains its pointing without a single thruster firing. In all three cases, it is not a "force" that works but simply the absence of moment.
steps.latex: \vec M = 0 \;\Longrightarrow\; \vec L = \mathrm{const} \;\Longrightarrow\; |\vec L| = \mathrm{const}\ \ \text{and}\ \ \hat L = \mathrm{const}
steps.figCaption: Zero moment preserves not only the magnitude $L$ but also the direction of the axis in space — on this rests all spin stabilization

steps.text:
Now turn on gravity. A top rests with its tip at point $O$, the axis is tilted from the vertical by angle $\theta$, and the center of mass lies on the axis at distance $a$ from the tip. The weight $m\vec g$ is applied at the center of mass and directed downward. The moment about the pivot is the cross product of the radius vector and the force.

The magnitude reads as force times lever arm, and here the lever arm is the horizontal distance from the vertical through the tip to the center of mass, i.e., $a\sin\theta$. The direction is given by the cross product rule: the result is perpendicular to both factors. Perpendicular to the weight — hence perpendicular to the vertical, hence strictly horizontal at any tilt. Perpendicular to the radius vector, which lies along the axis — hence perpendicular to $\vec L$, which also lies there. Remember both perpendicularities: the next step consists entirely of them.
steps.latex: \vec M = \vec r \times m\vec g, \qquad |\vec M| = m g a \sin\theta, \qquad \vec M \perp \vec L, \quad \vec M \perp \hat z
steps.figCaption: The lever arm of the weight is the horizontal distance $a\sin\theta$; the moment itself is perpendicular to both the axis and the vertical, i.e., horizontal

steps.text:
The key step, and it is entirely geometric. Only that part of the increment directed along the vector itself changes its length; the transverse part only rotates it. This is verified in one line: differentiate the squared length and get twice the dot product of the vector and its derivative. Since $\vec M \perp \vec L$, this product is zero — the length $L$ is constant, no matter what the weight does.

But this one perpendicularity is not enough: the axis could tilt without changing the length of $\vec L$. Here the second perpendicularity works. The moment is horizontal, so its vertical projection is zero, so the vertical component $L_z$ also does not change. Adding up: the length is constant, the vertical projection is constant, — hence their ratio $\cos\theta$ is constant. The tilt of the axis is locked. What remains to change is only the azimuth: the tip of the vector $\vec L$ moves along a horizontal circle, and the axis traces a cone about the vertical.

Here is the answer to the section's question. The top does not fall not because something props it from below, and not because rotation creates some new force. To fall means to increase $\theta$, and for that one must either shorten $\vec L$ or reduce its vertical part. A horizontal moment perpendicular to $\vec L$ can do neither.
steps.latex: \frac{d}{dt}\bigl(\vec L\cdot\vec L\bigr) = 2\,\vec L\cdot\frac{d\vec L}{dt} = 2\,\vec L\cdot\vec M = 0 \;\Longrightarrow\; L = \mathrm{const}; \qquad \frac{dL_z}{dt} = M_z = 0 \;\Longrightarrow\; \cos\theta = \frac{L_z}{L} = \mathrm{const}
steps.figCaption: The increment is horizontal and perpendicular to $\vec L$: neither the length of the vector nor its vertical projection changes — only an azimuthal rotation remains

steps.text:
Let us calculate the speed of this rotation. It is convenient to look from above: there only what moves is visible. The horizontal projection of the vector $\vec L$ has length $L\sin\theta$ — this is the radius of the circle along which the tip of the vector moves. In time $dt$, the tip shifts by $|d\vec L| = M\,dt$, and the shift is perpendicular to the projection, i.e., purely along the arc, adding nothing to the radius. The angle of rotation is the arc divided by the radius.

And here happens what was worth calculating. In the numerator is the moment $mga\sin\theta$, in the denominator the radius $L\sin\theta$. The sines cancel, and the tilt of the axis disappears from the answer completely. A top tilted almost horizontally goes around the vertical with exactly the same angular speed as a top standing almost upright. This is exactly the case where the formula knows more than intuition: on a stand this is checked with one move of the $\theta$ slider.
steps.latex: d\varphi = \frac{|d\vec L|}{L\sin\theta} = \frac{M\,dt}{L\sin\theta} \;\Longrightarrow\; \Omega = \frac{d\varphi}{dt} = \frac{M}{L\sin\theta} = \frac{mga\,\sin\theta}{I\omega\,\sin\theta} = \frac{mga}{I\omega}
steps.figCaption: Top view: in $dt$ the tip of the vector traverses an arc $M\,dt$ along a circle of radius $L\sin\theta$ — hence the angular speed of precession

steps.text:
Let us read the formula in words. In the numerator is everything that topples the top: mass, gravity, the offset of the center of mass. In the denominator is everything that resists: moment of inertia and intrinsic rotation. And the main consequence contradicts first impression — the faster the top is spun, the SLOWER it precesses. It seems that a fast one should also run sideways faster; in fact, the opposite, and the reason is visible from the derivation: in the same time, the same moment gives the same increment $d\vec L$, but it rotates a long vector by a smaller angle.

From here immediately follows how it all ends. Friction at the tip eats away $\omega$, the denominator melts, $\Omega$ grows — the axis begins to go around faster and faster. The accelerating precession before the fall is not the cause of the end but its herald.

Numbers on a bicycle wheel removed from the fork and suspended by one end of the axle. Mass $m = 2.0$ kg, almost all on the rim of radius $R = 0.35$ m, so $I = mR^{2}$ (first section, hoop coefficient $k = 1$). Spun up to $\omega = 30$ rad/s — about five revolutions per second. The rope holds the axle at distance $a = 0.25$ m from the wheel's center.
steps.latex: I = 0.245\ \text{kg·m}^2,\quad L = I\omega = 7.35\ \frac{\text{kg·m}^2}{\text{s}},\quad M = mga = 4.905\ \text{N·m}, \qquad \Omega = \frac{4.905}{7.35} = 0.667\ \frac{\text{rad}}{\text{s}}, \quad T = \frac{2\pi}{\Omega} = 9.4\ \text{s}
steps.figCaption: A wheel suspended by one end of the axle does not fall but goes around in nine and a half seconds — and in that time it manages to spin 45 times

steps.text:
The same formula on a planetary scale. The Earth is not a sphere: due to diurnal rotation, its equatorial radius is 21 kilometers larger than the polar one, and around the equator runs a bulge. The Moon and the Sun pull the near side of this bulge more strongly than the far side, and a moment results that tends to lay the equator into the orbital plane — i.e., to straighten the axis. But the moment is perpendicular to the axis, and we already know what such a moment does: the axis does not straighten but precesses, maintaining a tilt of 23.44° and going around in 25,772 years. The difference from the top here is in sign: for the top, gravity topples the axis, and the precession goes in the same direction as the top's spin, while the Moon and the Sun straighten the axis — the moment is directed oppositely, and the Earth's axis goes around against its own rotation. Astronomers call this the retrograde motion of the equinoxes.

Let us turn the formula around and find the moment responsible for this. The Earth's moment of inertia $I = 0.3307\,MR^{2} = 8.02\cdot10^{37}$ kg·m², angular velocity by sidereal day $\omega = 7.292\cdot10^{-5}$ rad/s, hence $L = 5.85\cdot10^{33}$ kg·m²/s. Precession speed: 50.29 arcseconds per year, i.e., $7.73\cdot10^{-12}$ rad/s. Now $M = \Omega L \sin\varepsilon$ — the same formula from step 6, but solved for the moment.

The answer must be checked independently, otherwise it is not a calculation but a fit. The moment from an attracting body is calculated directly: it is proportional to the difference of principal moments of inertia $C - A$, i.e., to that very non-sphericity. The Moon gives $1.24\cdot10^{22}$ N·m, the Sun — $0.57\cdot10^{22}$, the sum $1.81\cdot10^{22}$. It agrees with the first number to fractions of a percent, and at the same time the contribution of each is visible: the Moon is 2.2 times stronger than the Sun, although it yields to it in mass by 27 million times — it wins by the cube of the distance.
steps.latex: M = \Omega\,L\,\sin\varepsilon = 7.73\cdot10^{-12}\cdot 5.85\cdot10^{33}\cdot 0.398 = 1.80\cdot10^{22}\ \text{N·m}; \qquad \tfrac{3}{4}\,\frac{Gm}{r^{3}}\,(C-A)\sin 2\varepsilon\ \Big|_{\text{Moon}+\text{Sun}} = 1.81\cdot10^{22}\ \text{N·m}
steps.figCaption: The Earth's axis traces a cone with half-angle 23.44° in 25,772 years. The formula is the same as for the top — only the moment is created by the Moon and the Sun, and the role of the lever arm is played by the equatorial bulge

derivation.plateCap: On the left — how fast the axis goes around the vertical. On the right — what topples the top divided by what resists. The tilt of the axis is absent from the formula entirely: it canceled along the way, and this is the only truly unexpected result of the section.
derivation.note: Let us list what we silently assumed — these are the boundaries of the formula. First: $\vec L$ is directed strictly along the axis. Strictly, this is true only for a symmetric body rotating about a principal axis; in general, $\vec L$ and $\vec\omega$ are not parallel, and a completely different mechanics results — about that in the appendix. Second: the top is fast, i.e., $\Omega \ll \omega$, which is the same as $I\omega^{2} \gg mga$. For our wheel, the threshold $\sqrt{mga/I} = \sqrt{4.905/0.245} = 4.5$ rad/s at operating 30 — a nearly sevenfold margin. A slow top does not obey the formula. Third: we obtained a particular solution where $\theta$ is strictly constant; the general solution also contains nutation — a small trembling of the axis that a real top shows in the first half-second after launch. Fourth: there is no friction, $\omega$ is constant, the pivot is stationary. A real tip slides, rolls, and heats up, and it is precisely friction at the pivot that is responsible for the most beautiful effects — the rising boiled egg and the tumbling tippe-top toy.

math.title: The Math Needed Here
math.lead: There is almost no physics in this section—just three geometric facts about vectors. We'll cover them separately, because each one works far beyond the gyroscope.

items.what: Derivative of a vector: length and direction separately
items.why:
Any increment of a vector splits into two parts: along the vector itself and perpendicular to it. The first changes the length, the second only the direction, and nothing else. Formally, this is written via the derivative of the squared length: it equals twice the dot product of the vector and its derivative. If the derivative is perpendicular to the vector, the product is zero, and the length is constant. The converse is also true: if the length is constant, the derivative must be perpendicular.

This fact is the entire gyroscope in one line. But it also explains completely different things, because the vector in it can be anything. Take velocity: a force perpendicular to velocity does not change its magnitude—hence uniform circular motion, and hence the magnetic Lorentz force does no work. Take the radius vector: velocity perpendicular to it means motion along a circle of constant radius. The same math on three different vectors.
items.latex: \frac{d}{dt}\,|\vec A|^{2} = 2\,\vec A\cdot\frac{d\vec A}{dt} \qquad \Longrightarrow \qquad \Bigl(\frac{d\vec A}{dt} \perp \vec A\Bigr) \iff \bigl(|\vec A| = \mathrm{const}\bigr)

items.what: Cross product: where both perpendicularities come from
items.why:
Torque is defined via the cross product: its magnitude equals the product of the lengths times the sine of the angle between them, and its direction is perpendicular to both factors by the right-hand rule. In our problem, the factors are the radius vector along the top's axis and the vertical weight. Hence both perpendicularities of step 5 come for free, without any physics: perpendicular to the vertical (the torque is horizontal) and perpendicular to the axis (the torque is perpendicular to $\vec L$).

The sine of the angle gives another consequence worth checking by hand. When the axis becomes strictly vertical, the angle between the radius vector and the weight is zero, the sine is zero, there is no torque at all—and no precession either. Such a top is called sleeping: it stands straight and seems motionless. This state lives exactly until friction knocks it slightly sideways; then the sine ceases to be zero, and the top wakes up.
items.latex: \vec M = \vec r \times m\vec g, \qquad |\vec M| = m g a \sin\theta, \qquad \vec M \perp \vec r,\ \ \vec M \perp \vec g, \qquad \theta \to 0 \;\Longrightarrow\; \vec M \to 0

items.what: Angle as arc divided by radius—and a compact notation for all of precession
items.why:
In step 6, we computed the rotation angle as the ratio of arc to radius. This is the definition of a radian, and it works only for small angles, where the arc does not differ from the chord—and our angle is infinitesimal by construction, so there is no nitpicking. It is only important not to mix up the radius: the tip of the vector $\vec L$ does not travel along a circle of radius $L$, but along a horizontal circle of radius $L\sin\theta$, because the vertical component does not move.

Everything folds into one line that replaces the whole derivation. If a vector of constant length rotates about some axis with angular velocity $\vec\Omega$, then its derivative equals the cross product $\vec\Omega$ with the vector itself: the magnitude is exactly $\Omega L \sin\theta$, and the direction is perpendicular to both. Equate this to the torque—and you get the same precession formula in one line. Remember this notation: in the third section it will become a working tool, but here it is just a beautiful coincidence.
items.latex: \Omega = \frac{|d\vec L|}{L\sin\theta\;dt} \qquad \Longleftrightarrow \qquad \frac{d\vec L}{dt} = \vec\Omega \times \vec L, \quad \bigl|\vec\Omega \times \vec L\bigr| = \Omega L \sin\theta = M

example.title: Example with numbers
example.lead: Let's calculate a child's spinning top—and also find out at what rotation speed our formula stops being valid. The second part is more interesting than the first.
example.given: Spinning top: a disk of mass $m = 80$ g and radius $R = 3.0$ cm, mounted on a stem; the tip is 3.0 cm below the disk's center, so $a = 0.030$ m. The axis is tilted at $\theta = 20°$. Spun up to $\omega = 300$ rad/s—that's 48 revolutions per second. $g = 9.81$ m/s². Find the precession speed and period, then figure out what happens when friction reduces $\omega$ to 30 rad/s.
example.law: The disk's moment of inertia $I = \tfrac12 mR^{2}$ is taken ready-made from the first section. Then $L = I\omega$, $M = mga\sin\theta$, and $\Omega = mga/(I\omega)$—the formula from step 6.

solution.text: Moment of inertia. We neglect the stem's mass: it is small and mostly sits close to the axis, so it contributes little to $\sum m r^{2}$.
Angular momentum and torque due to gravity. Note: the torque came out small, eight thousandths of a newton-meter—but $L$ is also not large.

Precession speed. You can calculate it two ways—via $M/(L\sin\theta)$ or directly with the final formula, where the sine is already canceled. The answers must match, and this is a good check of your arithmetic.

Period of one revolution around the axis and the number of spin revolutions during that time. The ratio $\omega/\Omega$ also serves as a check of the fast-top condition: the larger it is, the more reliable the formula.

Now about slowing down. Friction reduces $\omega$, and the formula promises that $\Omega$ grows inversely proportionally: plugging in 30 rad/s gives 21.8 rad/s. This number can no longer be trusted—it is of the same order as the spin itself, while the whole derivation relied on the opposite, $\Omega \ll \omega$. Formally, $\Omega$ and $\omega$ become equal when $I\omega^{2} = mga$; this is a lower-bound estimate, the true boundary lies higher—the exact condition is discussed in the appendix.

example.answer: The top precesses at 2.18 rad/s and completes a circle in 2.9 seconds, managing to spin around its own axis 138 times in that interval. While the top is well spun up, the formula is accurate: at 300 rad/s the correction is about two percent. But it breaks down long before stopping—a rough estimate of the threshold gives 26 rad/s, the exact one (in the appendix) is about 78, i.e., roughly thirteen revolutions per second. Below this, the top still spins, but it no longer has a smooth precession around the vertical.
example.check:
Let's check in two ways. First, by eye: three seconds per revolution around the axis for a well-spun top is plausible—it's the slow, majestic motion you actually see.
\nSecond, by comparison with the wheel from step seven. The wheel's moment of inertia is 6800 times larger, but the torque due to gravity is only 208 times larger, and it is spun ten times slower. Multiplying the ratios: $\Omega_{\text{wheel}}/\Omega_{\text{top}} = 208 \cdot 10 / 6800 = 0.31$, meaning the wheel should precess three times slower than the top. And indeed: 0.667 versus 2.18, ratio 0.31. Two independent calculations agree—arithmetic is fine.
\nAnd an honest caveat about what the calculation omits. A real top's tip is not a point: it slides and rolls on the table, the support point wanders, and friction adds up, slowly raising the axis toward the vertical. A toy top usually doesn't tilt more and more; instead, it straightens up as it spins up—and that's not our formula but a separate effect of friction at the contact point, the same one that makes a hard-boiled egg stand up when spun.

constants.title: Constants of this section
constants.lead: All four are about the Earth, because the Earth is the main experimental specimen here: a top with a mass of six septillion kilograms that people have been observing for twenty-two centuries.

items.name: Angular velocity of Earth's rotation
items.why: It is calculated from the sidereal day — 86,164.1 seconds — not from the familiar 86,400. The difference of 3 minutes 56 seconds accumulates because during a day the Earth travels about a degree along its orbit, and to have the Sun again at the same point in the sky, it has to turn that extra degree. Astronomy lives by the sidereal day, everyday life by the solar day. The angular momentum of the Earth, which we calculate in step eight, includes precisely the sidereal value.
items.mnemo: Seven and three tenths times ten to the minus fifth is about 15 degrees per hour, exactly the separation between neighboring time zones. Hence the navigators' rule: an hour of longitude equals fifteen degrees.

items.name: Dimensionless moment of inertia of the Earth
items.why: For a uniform sphere this coefficient is exactly 0.4. For the Earth it is smaller — and this is direct evidence, based on nothing else, that the mass is concentrated toward the center: a heavy iron core under a light rocky mantle. The number is measured from precession and satellite motion, not from drilling, and historically it was the first quantitative argument for a metallic core. For comparison: the Moon has 0.394 — almost a uniform sphere, almost no core; the Sun has 0.070 — matter is pulled toward the center extraordinarily strongly.
items.mnemo: The smaller the coefficient, the more strongly the mass is concentrated toward the center. 0.4 — uniform sphere; 0.33 — Earth; 0.07 — Sun; 0 — a point.

items.name: Dynamic flattening of the Earth, $(C-A)/C$
items.why: The difference between the moment of inertia about the polar axis and about the equatorial axis, divided by the former. This is the non-sphericity that the Moon and Sun grab hold of: if the Earth were a perfect sphere, there would be no torque and no precession. Three thousandths look negligible, but they produce a torque of $1.8\cdot10^{22}$ N·m and all twenty-six thousand years. The reciprocal, 305, is also famous: Euler computed it as the period of free polar motion in days. Observed is 433 days, and the discrepancy is the price for the Earth not being a perfectly rigid body.
items.mnemo: Three thousandths — the entire geometric cause of precession. And its reciprocal, 305 days, is Euler's prediction, which nature corrected to 433.

items.name: Precession constant (general precession in longitude)
items.why: A full circle is 1,296,000 arcseconds; dividing by 50.29 gives 25,770 years, and with the unrounded 50.2877″ — the well-known 25,772 years. Over the two thousand years since the ancient catalogs, the vernal equinox point has moved by almost 28 degrees — that is, almost a full zodiac sign of 30 degrees. Hence the famous discrepancy: the astrological 'sign' and the constellation where the Sun actually is have drifted apart by about one item on the list. Strictly speaking, one distinguishes lunisolar precession (50.39″ per year — what our formula calculates) and general precession in longitude (50.29″); the difference is due to the slow rotation of the ecliptic plane itself from planetary attraction. We used 50.29, and for the estimate of the torque in step eight the choice affects only the third decimal: 1.796 versus 1.800.
items.mnemo: Fifty arcseconds per year is the apparent diameter of the Moon in about 37 years, that is, in one generation. Hipparchus noticed the shift because he compared his measurements with records from a century and a half earlier.

synthesis.title: How this connects to the rest of the course
synthesis.lead: The equation $d\vec L/dt = \vec M$ is one of the most far-reaching formulas in the course: it works equally well on a spinning top, a planet, a proton in a scanner, and a neutron star.

items.h: Moment of inertia (Section 1 of this topic)
items.text: Everything we used here — $I = kmR^{2}$ and the coefficients 1, ½, ⅖, 1/12 — was derived there and taken here as a given. From there also comes the equation $M = I\varepsilon$, which in the second step is simply rewritten in vector form. If the precession formula seems to come out of nowhere, look at it this way: the numerator is the torque from the first section, the denominator is the angular momentum assembled from the moment of inertia of that same first section.

The conservation of angular momentum is derived there from the isotropy of space, and there the figure skater who pulls in her arms and spins faster is analyzed. Here we use the same law from the other side: we are interested not in the fact that the length of $\vec L$ is conserved, but that its direction is conserved, and what happens when the torque is not zero.

The formula $d\vec A/dt = \vec\Omega \times \vec A$, which appeared here as a compact notation for precession, will become the main working tool there: applied twice, it gives the centrifugal and Coriolis forces. For now, remember it as a fact about a rotating vector — the body in Section 3 will be a point, and angular momentum will not be needed there at all.

A proton has its own angular momentum — spin — and an associated magnetic moment. In an external field, a torque acts on the magnetic moment, perpendicular to the spin, and then our derivation repeats exactly: the spin does not align with the field but precesses around it at a rate $\Omega = \gamma B$. In a field of 1.5 tesla, that is 64 million revolutions per second. An MRI scanner listens precisely to this precession, so a knee image is a direct application of the formula derived on a spinning top.

When the core of a massive star collapses into a neutron star, its radius shrinks by a factor of about 70,000. The moment of inertia scales as the square of the radius, angular momentum is conserved, so the angular velocity grows as the inverse square of the radius — by almost five billion times. From the Sun's 25 days, that would give more than two thousand revolutions per second. The fastest observed are around 716 — and that is an honest discrepancy: most of the angular momentum is carried away by the ejected envelope. The pulsar's axis, like that of any free top, holds its direction in space, and therefore its radiation reaches us as strictly periodic pulses.

In general relativity, a rotating mass drags space itself along, and a gyroscope hanging nearby experiences an additional torque. The effect was predicted by Josef Lense and Hans Thirring in 1918, and measured by the Gravity Probe B satellite, whose four ultra-precise gyroscopes drifted by 37.2 milliarcseconds over a year, with 39.2 predicted. The physics is different, but the equation is the same: $d\vec L/dt = \vec M$.

curiosities.title: Fun: try it with your hands
curiosities.lead: The two experiments below require a boiled egg and a book with a rubber band. Both demonstrate things that do not follow from our formula — and that is exactly why they are worth doing.

items.h: A boiled egg stands on its end
items.text: Boil an egg hard and cool it. Lay it on its side on a smooth table and spin it as fast as you can with your fingers. After a second or two, the egg will rise by itself and spin upright on its blunt end. A raw egg will not do the same — why is explained in the first paragraph: the liquid inside barely spins with the shell. You don't need a plate under the egg; nothing breaks; you just need a smooth, dry table.
items.answer:
The first thing to note: when the egg stands up, its center of mass RISES by about a centimeter. This is work against gravity, and it is done using rotational energy — after rising, the egg spins noticeably slower. So there must be a force that does this work, and there is: sliding friction at the point of contact. While the egg lies on its side and spins, the contact point slips on the table, and the friction force provides a torque that lifts the egg.

This is the only place in the paragraph where friction decides everything — in our derivation, it was absent altogether. And honestly, the full solution to this problem was obtained only in 2002. Keith Moffatt and Yasuhiro Shimomura published it in Nature, showing that the rising speed is determined by a single dimensionless condition linking rotation and friction, and that if spun too slowly, the egg will never stand up. The problem looks like a toy, yet it took longer to solve than many accelerator questions.

The same mechanism works in the tippe-top toy — a mushroom with a cut-off top that, when spun on its cap, flips over and stands on its stem, raising its center of mass by several centimeters.

items.text: Take a thick book, tie it with a rubber band across so it doesn't open in flight. Toss it a little above the sofa or bed, spinning it in three different ways: around the spine (the axis runs along the spine: the book rotates like a door on its hinges, only the axis is in the middle); flat like a frisbee, around an axis sticking out of the cover; and over the head, around a horizontal axis parallel to the top edge. The first two times, the book will calmly reach the sofa in the same rotation. The third time, it will inevitably flip around the spine — and it flips every time, no matter how you throw it.
items.answer:
The book has three dimensions, and each axis has its own moment of inertia. For our book 20 × 15 × 3 cm, the ratios come out to 2.67 : 1.75 : 1: the largest is around the axis sticking out of the cover, the smallest around the spine, and in the middle is exactly the axis around which the book refuses to spin. This is a general law: free rotation is stable around the axes of greatest and least moment of inertia and unstable around the middle, intermediate one. Poinsot proved this in 1834, and there is no special physics here — only that $\vec L$ is generally not parallel to $\vec\omega$, while in our derivation we assumed they were parallel.

It is easy to check that this is not a property of the book: the same flip is shown by a tennis racket, a TV remote, and a phone. The most famous recording was made in 1985 on the Salyut-7 station: cosmonaut Vladimir Dzhanibekov unscrewed a wing nut, it flew off into weightlessness, traveled a few centimeters, and tumbled, then again, then again — with a steady period. In weightlessness, where nothing interferes, the tumbles go on forever, and the phenomenon got the name of the Dzhanibekov effect.

items.h: Where does the energy of precession come from
items.text: A precessing wheel moves — so this motion has kinetic energy. But the torque of gravity is horizontal, the center of mass moves along a horizontal circle, and gravity does no work: the force is vertical, the displacement horizontal. The spin itself also gives nothing, $\omega$ is constant by condition. Where did the energy come from?
items.answer:
From a very short fall at the very beginning. When you release the wheel, it does not start precessing instantly: first the axis sags a little, and it is on this sagging that gravity does work. Then the axis rises back, sags again — this is nutation — the oscillations quickly damp out due to friction, and a steady precession remains at a slightly lower level.

The numbers match, but not as simply as one would like. The moment of inertia of our wheel about the transverse axis through the suspension point is $\tfrac12 mR^{2} + ma^{2} = 0.2475$ kg·m², and the kinetic energy of precession is $\tfrac12 \cdot 0.2475 \cdot 0.667^{2} = 0.055$ J. And the sagging turns out to be twice as generous as needed for one precession: to the average level, the axis drops by 1.3 degrees, i.e., the center of mass descends by 5.6 millimeters, and gravity gives off $mgh = 0.11$ J. The second half is not lost — nutation takes it: the oscillation of the axis goes at the same magnitude of speed as the precession, so it carries away exactly the same amount. Friction eats the nutation in a second, the axis remains at the average level, and the precession lives on with its 0.055 J. Nothing is lost and nothing is taken from nowhere.

It is useful to estimate the scale: the energy of the wheel's own rotation $\tfrac12 I\omega^{2} = 110$ J, so the precession carries away one two-thousandth of it, and together with nutation — one thousandth. That is why it can be considered free and why in the derivation we calmly wrote $\omega = \mathrm{const}$.

items.h: The North Star is a position, not a name
items.text: The Earth's axis traces a cone over 25,772 years, and with it, the north celestial pole moves across the sky. Today, near it is α Ursae Minoris, which we call the North Star. It was not always so and will not remain so.
items.answer:
In the time of the Egyptian pyramids, around 2700 BC, the celestial pole stood near Thuban — α Draconis, and it is toward it, according to one version, that the narrow shafts in the Great Pyramid of Giza are directed. The closest approach of the North Star to the pole will be around 2100 AD — at 27 arcminutes — and then it will begin to move away. In about 12,000 years, its place will be taken by Vega, one of the brightest stars in the sky, and the pole star will become truly noticeable.

Hipparchus discovered all this without knowing either the cause or what he had discovered: he simply compared his measurements of the longitude of Spica with the records of Timocharis made 150 years earlier, and found a discrepancy of two degrees, too large for an error. A century and a half of observations against one and a half degrees per century — a rare case where a discovery is made by patience, not instruments. The cause was named by Newton eighteen centuries later.

items.text: The rotor in a gimbal mount was for a century and a half the only way to remember a direction. Today, in a phone, in an airplane, and in a rocket, there are devices called gyroscopes inside which nothing rotates at all.
items.answer:
The mechanical gyroscope is wonderful as long as long-term operation is not needed. Its trouble is drift: any parasitic torque in the bearings, however small, according to the formula $\Omega = M/(I\omega)$ turns the axis, and the error accumulates linearly with time. A good aviation gyroscope drifts by a degree per hour, the best laboratory ones by hundredths of a degree; for a multi-hour flight without satellite correction, this is not enough.

The first workaround was the Sagnac effect: if you send two light beams around a ring in opposite directions, then when the ring rotates, the beams arrive with different travel times, and the difference is proportional to the angular velocity. No bearings, no inertia, nothing wears out. A laser gyroscope based on this principle has been on airplanes since the seventies, and a fiber-optic one — almost everywhere precision is needed.

In a phone, however, there is a third option — micromechanical: a silicon plate the size of a grain of sand oscillates, and the rotation of the device shifts the plane of its oscillations. Strictly speaking, this is no longer a gyroscope, but a measurer of the Coriolis effect, and it works on the physics of the third paragraph, not this one. Its accuracy is orders of magnitude worse than a laser one, but it costs a dollar and fits in a phone case — something no one could have expected from a Foucault top.

blocks.h: Nutation: a jitter that is not in our formula
blocks.text:
We obtained a particular solution — regular precession, where the tilt of the axis is strictly constant. The general solution also contains oscillations of $\theta$, called nutation. They are easy to see: if you release a tilted top from complete rest, without giving it a push in azimuth, it will first start to fall; the fall will spin up precession, precession will raise the axis back — and the tip of the axis will trace not a circle but a small cycloid. The frequency of these oscillations for a fast top is approximately $I\omega/I_\perp$, where $I_\perp$ is the moment of inertia about the transverse axis through the pivot point. For our wheel this is $0.245 \cdot 30 / 0.2475 = 29.7$ rad/s — almost $\omega$ itself, meaning the jitter is very fast and very small. Its amplitude is also calculated: an axis released from rest drops by $\Delta\theta = M I_\perp/(I\omega)^{2} = 1.3°$ to the average level and by twice that, 2.6°, at the lowest point of the swing. Friction damps these oscillations within a second, leaving a steady circular motion at the average level.

Earth also has nutation, and it has long been measured. Its main term is 9.2 arcseconds with a period of 18.6 years, and this period is not accidental: it is the time for one revolution of the nodes of the lunar orbit. The torque from the Moon is not constant precisely because the plane of its orbit slowly rotates. Nutation was discovered by James Bradley in 1748, after observing for exactly one such period.

blocks.h: Angular momentum is not always along the axis
blocks.text:
In the first step we wrote $\vec L = I\vec\omega$, as if $I$ were an ordinary number. In general this is not so: the moment of inertia is a tensor, and $\vec L$ is parallel to $\vec\omega$ only when rotation is about one of the three principal axes of the body. Every body has such axes — exactly three, mutually perpendicular — and they correspond to three principal moments of inertia $I_1 < I_2 < I_3$.

This leads to something our formula does not know at all: free rotation is stable about the axes with the largest and smallest moments and unstable about the intermediate one. This is the intermediate axis theorem, proved by Poinsot in 1834; in the kitchen it is demonstrated with a book and a rubber band, in space — with the Dzhanibekov nut. Earth also does not rotate strictly about its figure axis: the pole wanders in a spiral a few meters across with a period of 433 days. Euler predicted 305 days for a perfectly rigid Earth — this is $1/H$, the inverse of the dynamic flattening from the constants table — and the discrepancy with the observed 433 days is a measure of the fact that Earth is elastic, not rigid.
blocks.latex: \vec L = \hat I\,\vec\omega, \qquad \vec L \parallel \vec\omega \iff \vec\omega\ \text{along a principal axis}; \qquad I_1 < I_2 < I_3:\ \text{rotation about } I_2\ \text{is unstable}

blocks.h: The top slows down, but we assumed ω constant
blocks.text:
Strictly speaking, the formula $\Omega = mga/(I\omega)$ is derived for constant $\omega$, but for a real top it decreases. The quasi-stationary approximation saves us: as long as friction is small compared to the rotation itself, the formula can be applied at each moment, substituting the current $\omega(t)$. This is exactly how the observed picture is obtained — the axis traces increasingly faster circles.

But the approximation has a bottom. The condition for a fast top, $I\omega^{2} \gg mga$, is eventually violated, and a rough estimate of the threshold is $\omega_{*} = \sqrt{mga/I}$: for the top from the example it is 25.6 rad/s, for the wheel 4.5 rad/s. This estimate is too low, and it is more honest to state where the real boundary is. If we do not discard the transverse moment of inertia, the condition for the existence of regular precession looks like this: $(I\omega)^{2} \ge 4\,I_\perp\,mga\cos\theta$. For the top at a tilt of 20°, the transverse moment about the tip is $\tfrac14 mR^{2} + ma^{2} = 9.0\cdot10^{-5}$ kg·m², and the condition gives not 26 but about 78 rad/s — three times the rough estimate. And for the wheel the axis is horizontal, the cosine is zero, the right-hand side vanishes entirely: a regular solution exists at any spin, but the catch is that at slow spin one still has to get into it — nutation will not be a small ripple but a full-scale wobble of the axis. Below the threshold, precession becomes comparable to the intrinsic rotation, nutation ceases to be a small correction, and there is no longer any 'tilt is constant' — the top falls over. Along with that, the last assumption disappears: the pivot point is not ideal, the tip slides and rolls, and this friction separately raises or lowers the axis — an effect that stands a boiled egg on end and flips a tippe top.

Both estimates of the eighth step are honestly independent — one comes from the observed precession period, the other from the law of gravitation — but both rely on the same quantity $C - A$, the difference of Earth's principal moments of inertia. The agreement to fractions of a percent therefore checks the arithmetic and the model of Earth's shape, not the theory of gravitation itself.

What is missing from the calculation. We averaged the torque over the orbits of the Moon and the Sun, thereby discarding all nutation. We did not distinguish between luni-solar precession (50.39″ per year) and general precession in longitude (50.29″): the difference is due to the slow rotation of the ecliptic plane itself caused by planetary attraction. We treated Earth as rigid, whereas the oceans, the liquid outer core, and the viscous mantle respond to the tidal torque in their own ways, and modern precession models are already geophysics, not top mechanics. Finally, there is a relativistic addition: the geodetic precession of Earth's axis is about 19 milliarcseconds per year against 50,290 milliarcseconds of the main effect — 2,500 times smaller, but it has been measured and is included in modern astronomical standards.

memo.essence: Angular momentum $\vec L = I\vec\omega$ is a vector along the axis. The equation $d\vec L/dt = \vec M$ says that torque adds to it an increment in ITS direction. For a heavy top, the torque is horizontal and perpendicular to $\vec L$, so it can neither shorten the vector nor reduce its vertical component: the tilt of the axis is locked, only the azimuth changes. The speed of this motion is $\Omega = mga/(I\omega)$, and the tilt does not enter it.

keyIdeas.title: $\Omega = mga/(I\omega)$
keyIdeas.text: The faster the top spins, the SLOWER it precesses: $\omega$ is in the denominator

keyIdeas.title: Two perpendicularities
keyIdeas.text: $\vec M \perp \vec L$ keeps the vector's length, $\vec M \perp$ vertical keeps its vertical projection. Together they lock the tilt

keyIdeas.title: The tilt canceled out
keyIdeas.text: $\sin\theta$ appears both in the torque and in the turning radius, so the angle does not enter the precession speed at all

keyIdeas.title: Earth is the same top
keyIdeas.text: 25,772 years, tilt 23.44°, torque from the Moon and Sun on the equatorial bulge $1.8\cdot10^{22}$ N·m

where: Bicycle wheel on a rope: the axle does not fall but goes around a circle in 9.4 seconds
Rifled bullet and frisbee: zero torque keeps the axis direction, and the body does not tumble
Gyrocompass and aviation gyroscope: the axis remembers its direction, and drift is calculated with the same $\Omega = M/(I\omega)$
Precession of Earth's axis: 50.3 arcseconds per year, change of the pole star, shift of the zodiac by one sign
Magnetic resonance imaging: the proton spin precesses in a 1.5 T field at 64 MHz
memo.watchOut: Three traps. First, thinking that $\vec L$ points where the body's points run; it points along the axis, and the right-hand rule here is not a decoration but a definition. Second, expecting that a fast-spinning top will also move sideways faster; it is the opposite, $\omega$ is in the denominator. Third, applying the formula to a slow top: it is valid only when $I\omega^{2} \gg mga$, and below the threshold $\sqrt{mga/I}$ precession becomes comparable to the spin itself, and there is no constant tilt anymore.

quiz.q: The axis of a spinning top is tilted, gravity pulls the center of mass down, and the torque about the tip is not zero. Why doesn't the axis fall?
options: The torque is horizontal: it can neither change the length of $\vec L$ nor reduce its vertical component, and lowering the axis requires one of the two
The torque of gravity is balanced by the reaction force at the pivot, so the net torque is zero
The centrifugal force arising during rotation lifts the axis and compensates gravity
The axis actually does fall, just so slowly that it is imperceptible during the observation time
quiz.why:
The tilt of the axis is determined by the ratio of the vertical projection $L_z$ to the length $L$. The torque is horizontal, so its vertical projection is zero and $L_z$ does not change; the torque is perpendicular to $\vec L$, so the length does not change either. The ratio is constant, the tilt is locked, only the azimuth is free.

The answer about balanced torques is checked in one line: the reaction force is applied at the pivot point itself, its lever arm relative to that point is zero, so it produces no torque at all. The centrifugal force option is wrong because no such force exists in an inertial frame—inertial forces appear only when switching to a rotating frame, as mentioned in the third paragraph; moreover, it would be directed away from the axis, not upward. The 'falls imperceptibly' option describes a real top, but for a different reason: a real axis does slowly droop, but due to friction, which is absent in our derivation, whereas an ideal top keeps its tilt strictly forever.
quiz.hint: Lowering the axis means increasing the angle $\theta$, i.e., decreasing $\cos\theta = L_z/L$. Look at which two quantities must change for that, and ask whether a horizontal torque can change either of them.

quiz.q: The same top is spun twice as fast—everything else unchanged. What happens to the precession rate?
options: It halves
It doubles
It stays the same: the torque of gravity is the same
It quadruples
quiz.why:
$\Omega = mga/(I\omega)$—the spin angular velocity is in the denominator, so precession is inversely proportional to spin. You can understand this without the formula: in time $dt$, the torque gives the same increment $d\vec L = \vec M\,dt$, but it now rotates a vector twice as long, so by half the angle.

The 'doubles' option is the most common intuitive error in this topic: it seems that a fast top should also run sideways faster. The 'stays the same' option is true for the torque, but not for precession: the numerator is indeed the same, but the denominator has changed. You can also check this by eye—a dying top darts across the table much faster than a freshly spun one, even though the torque of gravity is exactly the same.
quiz.hint: Write down the formula and see whether $\omega$ is in the numerator or denominator. Then check yourself by observation: how does a top behave just before it falls, when the spin has almost died?

quiz.q: In your own words: why can a torque perpendicular to the vector $\vec L$ not change the length of that vector, but only rotate it?
quiz.why:
The increment of a vector can be decomposed into two parts: one along the vector itself and one across it. Only the first lengthens or shortens, the second purely rotates. If the increment is entirely perpendicular, there is simply no longitudinal part, so the length remains unchanged.

Formally, it is one line: the derivative of the squared length equals twice the dot product of the vector and its derivative, and the dot product of perpendicular vectors is zero. The converse is also true—if the length is constant, the derivative must be perpendicular.

It is useful to note that the vector here can be anything. The same reasoning explains why a force perpendicular to velocity does not change its magnitude: hence uniform circular motion, and also why the magnetic force does no work.
quiz.hint: Decompose the increment into two components—along the vector and across—and ask what each does. Or compute the derivative of $\vec L \cdot \vec L$.

quiz.q: A bicycle wheel of mass 2.0 kg with moment of inertia $I = 0.245$ kg·m² is spun up to $\omega = 30$ rad/s and hung by the end of its axle at a distance $a = 0.10$ m from the wheel's center. What is the angular velocity of precession? Answer in rad/s, $g = 9.81$ m/s².
quiz.why:
$\Omega = mga/(I\omega) = 2.0 \cdot 9.81 \cdot 0.10 / (0.245 \cdot 30) = 1.962/7.35 = 0.267$ rad/s. The period of the axis's orbit is $T = 2\pi/\Omega = 23.5$ s—almost half a minute per revolution.

A check without a calculator: in step seven, with a lever arm of 0.25 m, the result was 0.667 rad/s. Here the lever arm is 2.5 times smaller, and it enters the formula linearly, so the answer should also be 2.5 times smaller: $0.667/2.5 = 0.267$. It matches.

Also check the fast-top condition: $\sqrt{mga/I} = \sqrt{1.962/0.245} = 2.8$ rad/s against the working 30—a more than tenfold margin, so the formula applies confidently.
quiz.hint: Everything is directly in the formula $\Omega = mga/(I\omega)$: plug in the numbers and don't forget that $a$ is the distance from the pivot to the center of mass, not the wheel's radius.

formula.name: Momento angular y velocidad de precesión
formula.alsoKnown: Ecuación de momentos en forma vectorial; fórmula de la precesión regular de una peonza simétrica pesada. Para la Tierra, el mismo fenómeno se llama precesión de los equinoccios

authors.what: comparó sus mediciones de la posición de Espiga con los registros de Timocares, hechos un siglo y medio antes, y descubrió que el punto del equinoccio de primavera se desplaza a lo largo de la eclíptica no menos de un grado por siglo. La cautela en la formulación era apropiada: la velocidad real es de 1,4 grados por siglo. Descubrió el fenómeno, pero no conoció las causas

en el tercer libro de los 'Principia' explicó la precesión de los equinoccios por la atracción de la Luna y el Sol sobre el abultamiento ecuatorial de la Tierra. Este es el primer cálculo de un giroscopio en la historia, y se hizo directamente sobre un planeta, siglo y medio antes de que se construyera un giroscopio sobre una mesa

en 'Teoría del movimiento de los cuerpos sólidos' escribió las ecuaciones de rotación en ejes fijos al cuerpo, introdujo los ejes principales de inercia y los ángulos que llevan su nombre; de estas ecuaciones, la precesión y la nutación se obtienen como soluciones particulares

construyó un rotor rápido en un soporte cardán, mostró que su eje mantiene la dirección mientras la habitación gira junto con la Tierra, y le dio al dispositivo su nombre: gyroscope, 'el que mira la rotación'

formula.story:
Entre el descubrimiento y la explicación pasaron dieciocho siglos, y entre la explicación y la explicación correcta, otros sesenta años. Newton en los 'Principia' obtuvo un número casi correcto para la precesión del eje terrestre, pero en el camino se equivocó dos veces: pensó que la Luna actúa sobre el abultamiento de la Tierra aproximadamente cuatro veces y media más fuerte que el Sol, mientras que la relación real es un poco más del doble, y al mismo tiempo estimó incorrectamente el propio abultamiento. Los errores se compensaron parcialmente entre sí, y el resultado se pareció a la verdad. La derivación rigurosa la dio Jean Le Rond d'Alembert en 1749, y es a partir de él que se suele contar la teoría de la precesión como un cálculo, no como una conjetura.

El dispositivo apareció después de la teoría. Foucault en 1851 demostró la rotación de la Tierra con un péndulo, y al año siguiente quiso mostrar lo mismo sin una cuerda larga y una cúpula alta. Tomó un disco pesado, lo hizo girar a varios cientos de revoluciones por segundo y lo suspendió en un soporte cardán, donde ningún momento podía alcanzarlo. El eje mantenía la dirección, mientras todo el laboratorio giraba lentamente respecto a él. El experimento resultó poco convincente por una razón puramente técnica: la fricción en los cojinetes consumía la rotación en pocos minutos, y no se pudo medir nada cuantitativamente. Quedó el nombre. Medio siglo después, Hermann Anschütz-Kaempfe abordó el problema para el cual la brújula magnética no sirve en absoluto: la navegación dentro del casco de acero de un submarino, y en 1908 construyó un girocompás funcional. Desde ese momento, el giroscopio pasó de ser un juguete de demostración a un dispositivo sin el cual ningún avión vuela y ningún cohete alcanza la órbita.

symbols.what: momento de inercia respecto al eje de rotación
symbols.note: se toma de la primera sección: $I = kmR^2$, donde $k$ es 1 para un aro, ½ para un disco, ⅖ para una esfera
también un vector a lo largo del eje; para un cuerpo simétrico que gira alrededor del eje principal, $\vec L$ y $\vec\omega$ son paralelos; en el caso general no lo son

derivation.title: Derivación rigurosa
derivation.lead: Del primer apartado solo necesitamos dos cosas: la definición de momento de inercia $I$ y la ecuación de rotación $M = I\varepsilon$. Ambas se toman como dadas, no las vamos a redescubrir. Todo lo demás en esta derivación no es física, sino geometría de vectores: dos perpendicularidades y un arco.

steps.text:
Tomemos un cuerpo que gira alrededor de un eje fijo con velocidad angular $\omega$. Cada punto tiene un momento lineal $m_i v_i$ y un brazo $r_i$: la distancia al eje. La suma de los productos del momento lineal por el brazo se llama momento angular respecto al eje. Sustituimos $v_i = \omega r_i$ del primer apartado, y la suma conocida se factoriza sola: es el mismo momento de inercia $I$.

Pero $L$ no es un número, sino un vector, y su dirección es la fuente de la mitad de la confusión en este tema. Apunta A LO LARGO DEL EJE, no hacia donde corren los puntos del cuerpo. La elección no es arbitraria: la dirección del eje es la única dirección en el cuerpo que la rotación deja en su lugar; todas las demás giran con él, y solo a lo largo del eje se puede dibujar una flecha que no se escape. Hacia dónde a lo largo del eje lo determina la regla de la mano derecha: dobla los dedos en el sentido de la rotación y el pulgar señalará $\vec L$.
steps.latex: L = \sum_i m_i v_i r_i = \sum_i m_i \omega r_i^{2} = \Bigl(\sum_i m_i r_i^{2}\Bigr)\,\omega = I\omega, \qquad \vec L = I\vec\omega
steps.figCaption: Los puntos de la llanta corren en círculo, pero el vector $\vec L$ apunta a lo largo del eje: es la única dirección que la rotación deja en su lugar

steps.text:
Diferenciemos esta igualdad con respecto al tiempo. El cuerpo es rígido, el eje es el mismo, por lo tanto $I$ es constante y sale de la derivada. Queda la derivada de la velocidad angular: la aceleración angular $\vec\varepsilon$, y el producto $I\vec\varepsilon$ ya lo conocemos: es el momento de las fuerzas externas, la ecuación de rotación del primer apartado.

Formalmente no hemos escrito nada nuevo. En cuanto al contenido, lo hemos escrito todo. La forma escalar $M = I\varepsilon$ solo puede responder a una pregunta: más rápido o más lento. La forma vectorial responde además a la pregunta "hacia dónde girará el eje", que es la que nos ocupa. Hay que leerla literalmente y sin corregirla con el sentido común: en el tiempo $dt$ el vector $\vec L$ recibe un incremento $d\vec L = \vec M\,dt$ dirigido HACIA DONDE MIRA EL MOMENTO. No hacia donde mira el propio $\vec L$, ni hacia donde tira la fuerza.
steps.latex: \frac{d\vec L}{dt} = I\,\frac{d\vec\omega}{dt} = I\vec\varepsilon = \vec M \qquad \Longrightarrow \qquad d\vec L = \vec M\,dt
steps.figCaption: El incremento se suma al vector según la regla del paralelogramo y se dirige a lo largo del momento, no a lo largo del propio $\vec L$

steps.text:
Primero analicemos el caso simple: no hay momento externo. Entonces $\vec L$ es constante, y la constancia de un vector implica la constancia de dos cosas: su longitud y su dirección. La longitud se menciona más a menudo (la patinadora que junta los brazos se analiza en el tema "Leyes de conservación"), pero en la tecnología casi siempre funciona la segunda parte: un cuerpo giratorio que vuela libremente mantiene su eje en el espacio.

Una bala con estrías: el paso de estría es de 25 centímetros a una velocidad de 800 m/s, lo que da 3200 revoluciones por segundo, es decir, $\omega \approx 2\cdot10^{4}$ rad/s: ciento noventa mil revoluciones por minuto. El eje de esa bala se mantiene a lo largo de la trayectoria, y la bala no da vueltas de campana, sino que va de punta. Un frisbee a diez revoluciones por segundo mantiene su plano y por eso planea, no se cae. Un satélite, girado alrededor de un eje apuntando a un punto deseado, mantiene la orientación sin encender ni un solo motor. En los tres casos no actúa una "fuerza", sino simplemente la ausencia de momento.
steps.latex: \vec M = 0 \;\Longrightarrow\; \vec L = \mathrm{const} \;\Longrightarrow\; |\vec L| = \mathrm{const}\ \ \text{y}\ \ \hat L = \mathrm{const}
steps.figCaption: El momento nulo conserva no solo la magnitud $L$, sino también la dirección del eje en el espacio: en esto se basa toda la estabilización por rotación

steps.text:
Ahora incluyamos la gravedad. La peonza se apoya en la punta en el punto $O$, el eje está inclinado respecto a la vertical un ángulo $\theta$, el centro de masa está en el eje a una distancia $a$ de la punta. El peso $m\vec g$ está aplicado en el centro de masa y dirigido hacia abajo. El momento respecto al punto de apoyo es igual al producto vectorial del radio vector por la fuerza.

El módulo se lee como fuerza por brazo, y aquí el brazo es la distancia horizontal desde la vertical que pasa por la punta hasta el centro de masa, es decir, $a\sin\theta$. La dirección la da la regla del producto vectorial: el resultado es perpendicular a ambos factores. Es perpendicular al peso, por lo tanto perpendicular a la vertical, por lo tanto estrictamente horizontal para cualquier inclinación. Es perpendicular al radio vector, que está a lo largo del eje, por lo tanto también perpendicular a $\vec L$, que está en el mismo lugar. Recuerde ambas perpendicularidades: el siguiente paso consiste enteramente en ellas.
steps.latex: \vec M = \vec r \times m\vec g, \qquad |\vec M| = m g a \sin\theta, \qquad \vec M \perp \vec L, \quad \vec M \perp \hat z
steps.figCaption: El brazo del peso es la distancia horizontal $a\sin\theta$; el momento mismo es perpendicular tanto al eje como a la vertical, es decir, horizontal

steps.text:
El paso clave, y es completamente geométrico. La longitud de un vector solo la cambia la parte del incremento que es paralela a él; la parte transversal solo lo hace girar. Se comprueba en una línea: diferenciamos el cuadrado de la longitud y obtenemos el doble del producto escalar del vector por su derivada. Como $\vec M \perp \vec L$, ese producto es cero: la longitud $L$ es constante, haga lo que haga el peso.

Pero esta perpendicularidad no basta: el eje podría inclinarse sin cambiar la longitud de $\vec L$. Aquí actúa la segunda perpendicularidad. El momento es horizontal, por lo tanto su proyección vertical es cero, por lo tanto la componente vertical $L_z$ tampoco cambia. Sumamos: la longitud es constante, la proyección vertical es constante, por lo tanto también lo es su cociente $\cos\theta$. La inclinación del eje está bloqueada. Solo queda el azimut: el extremo del vector $\vec L$ recorre una circunferencia horizontal, y el eje describe un cono alrededor de la vertical.

Aquí está la respuesta a la pregunta del apartado. La peonza no se cae no porque algo la sostenga desde abajo, ni porque la rotación cree una nueva fuerza. Caer significa aumentar $\theta$, y para eso hay que acortar $\vec L$ o disminuir su componente vertical. El momento horizontal, perpendicular a $\vec L$, no puede hacer ni lo uno ni lo otro.
steps.latex: \frac{d}{dt}\bigl(\vec L\cdot\vec L\bigr) = 2\,\vec L\cdot\frac{d\vec L}{dt} = 2\,\vec L\cdot\vec M = 0 \;\Longrightarrow\; L = \mathrm{const}; \qquad \frac{dL_z}{dt} = M_z = 0 \;\Longrightarrow\; \cos\theta = \frac{L_z}{L} = \mathrm{const}
steps.figCaption: El incremento es horizontal y perpendicular a $\vec L$: no cambian ni la longitud del vector ni su proyección vertical; solo queda la rotación en azimut

steps.text:
Calculemos la velocidad de esa rotación. Es más fácil mirar desde arriba: allí solo se ve lo que se mueve. La proyección horizontal del vector $\vec L$ tiene longitud $L\sin\theta$: es el radio de la circunferencia por la que se mueve el extremo del vector. En el tiempo $dt$ el extremo se desplaza $|d\vec L| = M\,dt$, y el desplazamiento es perpendicular a la proyección, es decir, va puramente a lo largo del arco, sin añadir nada al radio. El ángulo de giro es el arco dividido por el radio.

Y aquí ocurre lo que valía la pena calcular. En el numerador está el momento $mga\sin\theta$, en el denominador el radio $L\sin\theta$. Los senos se cancelan y la inclinación del eje desaparece por completo de la respuesta. Una peonza casi tumbada recorre la vertical exactamente con la misma velocidad angular que una casi vertical. Este es precisamente el caso en que la fórmula sabe más que la intuición: en el banco de pruebas se comprueba con un solo movimiento del deslizador $\theta$.
steps.latex: d\varphi = \frac{|d\vec L|}{L\sin\theta} = \frac{M\,dt}{L\sin\theta} \;\Longrightarrow\; \Omega = \frac{d\varphi}{dt} = \frac{M}{L\sin\theta} = \frac{mga\,\sin\theta}{I\omega\,\sin\theta} = \frac{mga}{I\omega}
steps.figCaption: Vista superior: en $dt$ el extremo del vector recorre un arco $M\,dt$ sobre una circunferencia de radio $L\sin\theta$: de ahí la velocidad angular de precesión

steps.text:
Leamos la fórmula con palabras. En el numerador está todo lo que tumba la peonza: masa, gravedad, desplazamiento del centro de masa. En el denominador todo lo que se resiste: momento de inercia y rotación propia. Y la consecuencia principal contradice la primera impresión: cuanto más rápido gira la peonza, MÁS LENTA es su precesión. Parece que la rápida debería correr también más rápido hacia un lado; en realidad es al revés, y la razón se ve en la derivación: en el mismo tiempo, el mismo momento da el mismo incremento $d\vec L$, pero hace girar un vector largo un ángulo menor.

De aquí se deduce también cómo termina todo. La fricción en la punta consume $\omega$, el denominador se derrite, $\Omega$ crece: el eje empieza a recorrer el círculo cada vez más rápido. La precesión acelerada antes de la caída no es la causa del final, sino su precursor.

Números con una rueda de bicicleta, desmontada de la horquilla y suspendida por un extremo del eje. Masa $m = 2{,}0$ kg, casi toda en la llanta de radio $R = 0{,}35$ m, por lo tanto $I = mR^{2}$ (primer apartado, coeficiente del aro $k = 1$). Girada a $\omega = 30$ rad/s: unas cinco revoluciones por segundo. La cuerda sostiene el eje a una distancia $a = 0{,}25$ m del centro de la rueda.
steps.latex: I = 0{,}245\ \text{kg·m}^2,\quad L = I\omega = 7{,}35\ \frac{\text{kg·m}^2}{\text{s}},\quad M = mga = 4{,}905\ \text{N·m}, \qquad \Omega = \frac{4{,}905}{7{,}35} = 0{,}667\ \frac{\text{rad}}{\text{s}}, \quad T = \frac{2\pi}{\Omega} = 9{,}4\ \text{s}
steps.figCaption: La rueda, suspendida por un extremo del eje, no se cae, sino que recorre un círculo en nueve segundos y medio, y en ese tiempo gira 45 veces

steps.text:
La misma fórmula a escala planetaria. La Tierra no es una esfera: debido a la rotación diaria, su radio ecuatorial es 21 kilómetros mayor que el polar, y alrededor del ecuador hay un abultamiento. La Luna y el Sol tiran del lado cercano de ese abultamiento con más fuerza que del lejano, y se produce un momento que tiende a poner el ecuador en el plano de la órbita, es decir, a enderezar el eje. Pero el momento es perpendicular al eje, y ya sabemos lo que hace ese momento: el eje no se endereza, sino que precesa, manteniendo la inclinación de 23,44° y recorriendo el círculo en 25 772 años. La diferencia con la peonza está en el signo: en la peonza, la gravedad tumba el eje y el recorrido va en el mismo sentido en que gira la peonza, mientras que la Luna y el Sol enderezan el eje: el momento está dirigido en sentido opuesto, y el eje terrestre recorre el círculo en sentido contrario a su propia rotación. Los astrónomos llaman a esto movimiento retrógrado de los equinoccios.

Demos la vuelta a la fórmula y encontremos el momento responsable. El momento de inercia de la Tierra es $I = 0{,}3307\,MR^{2} = 8{,}02\cdot10^{37}$ kg·m², la velocidad angular según el día sidéreo es $\omega = 7{,}292\cdot10^{-5}$ rad/s, de donde $L = 5{,}85\cdot10^{33}$ kg·m²/s. La velocidad de precesión: 50,29 segundos de arco por año, es decir, $7{,}73\cdot10^{-12}$ rad/s. Ahora $M = \Omega L \sin\varepsilon$: la misma fórmula del paso 6, pero resuelta para el momento.

La respuesta hay que verificarla de forma independiente; si no, no es un cálculo, sino un ajuste. El momento debido al cuerpo atractor se calcula directamente: es proporcional a la diferencia de los momentos de inercia principales $C - A$, es decir, a esa misma falta de esfericidad. La Luna da $1{,}24\cdot10^{22}$ N·m, el Sol $0{,}57\cdot10^{22}$, la suma $1{,}81\cdot10^{22}$.
